Colour in this system is a rank, not a palette.
Every value here answers one question — how far forward does this sit, and is it asking for a decision. That is the line against Typography and Elevation: type carries structure, colour carries rank, and depth is drawn with a hairline rather than a shadow. When a screen looks flat and still reads in order, colour did the work.
01 Roles SEVEN
ROLE WHEN
{{ r.n }} {{ r.tok }}
{{ r.u }}
There is no success colour. Work that finished says so in a word and then gets out of the way — if every good outcome were green, the one bad one would have to shout louder than this interface allows.
02 Usage AMBER · NOT AMBER
Reach for amber when
The view has one action the operator is there to take. Something is live right now and the operator has to know. Focus has landed somewhere and the ring has to be unmistakable. A row, tab or step is the current one among several.
Use something else when
It informs rather than asks — that is Ice. It failed and needs naming — that is the alarm colour, plus the word. It is one of several series in a chart — hue there means identity, not urgency. You only want it noticed sooner — that is Typography, not another accent.

Two typefaces, six steps, and no decision left to make at the point of use.
Space Grotesk is structure — headings, numerals, anything the eye should land on first. IBM Plex Mono is everything else, which is why the shell reads like an instrument rather than a website. This page owns the metrics: which sizes exist, how they are tracked and led, and when each one is legal. What a block of copy is made of — eyebrow, heading, body, caption — belongs to the Text component.
01 Scale SIX STEPS
{{ t.n }} {{ t.sample }} {{ t.spec }}
Six steps and no half sizes. The gaps are wide enough that two adjacent ranks are never mistaken for each other, which is what lets the system get away with so little colour.
{{ a.n }}
{{ a.b }}
02 Families TWO
FAMILY WHEN
Space Grotesk 214 nominal 600 only · -.02em to -.01em
Headings, workspace names, and every number an operator reads as a quantity. One weight, always 600 — the family earns its place by being the only thing on the page that is not mono, so a second weight would only blur that signal.
IBM Plex Mono Four stages finished 400 only · 0 to .2em
Body, labels, table cells, code, timestamps, IDs — the default for anything that is not a heading. Its fixed advance is the reason columns of values line up without a tabular variant, and the reason the interface reads as a console.
There is no third family and no italic. Emphasis inside a sentence is carried by --fg against --dim, never by a slant the mono does not draw well.
03 Usage GROTESK · NOT GROTESK
Set it in Grotesk when
It names the thing the screen is about — a page, a workspace, a section. It is a number the operator is meant to read as a result, not as data in a cell. It is the first thing that should be found when the eye lands. It is one line. Grotesk is never used for a paragraph.
Use the mono when
It is read rather than scanned — any sentence, any description. It sits in a column with other values and has to align. It is a code, an ID, a path or a timestamp the operator may copy. It is a label above a panel, which is Label at .16em and uppercase.

Space is how this system groups things, and it does that job before any line is drawn.
Nine steps, comfortable density, no toggle. Two elements belong together because the gap between them is smaller than the gap around them — a border is only ever the second explanation. That is the line against Elevation: if a group still needs a hairline after the spacing is right, the hairline is doing structural work it should not have to do.
01 Scale NINE STEPS
STEP SIZE WHERE
{{ s.v }} {{ s.u }}
The steps crowd together at the bottom and spread out at the top on purpose: small distances are read as relationships and need fine control, large ones are read as separation and only need to be unmistakable.
02 Roles FOUR
ROLE WHEN
{{ r.n }} {{ r.tok }}
{{ r.u }}
There is no density setting. Comfortable is the only mode, decided once in code, because a system that ships two densities has to be designed twice and is usually only tested once.
03 Usage SPACE · NOT SPACE
Add space when
Two groups are being read as one because their gaps are equal. A control is close enough to another that a mis-click is plausible. A block of copy runs long and needs a resting point before the next one. A panel's contents touch its edge — inset is the first thing to fix.
Use something else when
Two groups must be adjacent and still distinct — that is a line. The gap is only there to make something look important — that is Typography. Lines inside a paragraph feel tight — that is leading, not spacing. You have run out of room. Cutting an element beats shaving a step.

09 Changelog THREE RELEASES
{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.b }}
Every surface in this system is 2px, and that is not a default — it is the lock.
There is no radius scale, so a corner never carries meaning: two elements with different corners are different kinds of thing, not different levels of importance. That is why only two shapes are allowed off 2px, and both of them are read as objects rather than surfaces — the fully rounded Chip, and the circle used for dots and avatars.
01 Values THREE · LOCKED
VALUE WHEN
2px .ds · every surface
Cards, panels, buttons, inputs, menus, modals, badges, table cells, swatches — anything that behaves as a surface. Enough to take the raw edge off a hairline at 1× and invisible at a glance, which is the point: the corner should never be the thing you notice.
20px FLEET ✕ Chips only
Chips, and nothing else. The full round is the tell that a thing can be picked up, toggled or thrown away — it is the one place where shape carries a behaviour, which is exactly why no other component may borrow it.
50% Dots · avatars · markers
Status dots, avatars and the numbered markers in a diagram. These are marks rather than containers — they hold no layout and take no padding, so a circle costs nothing and reads instantly at 8px.
There is no 4px, no 6px, and no large radius for large surfaces. A modal has the same corner as a badge because both are surfaces, and scaling the radius with the box is how a system ends up with eleven of them.
02 Usage SHARP · ROUND
2px, which is almost always
It contains something — padding, rows, a layout of any kind. It has a border, a fill, or both. It sits flush against another surface and has to align with it. You are unsure. 2px is the answer to every corner question by default.
Round it only when
It is a Chip — pickable, dismissible, or a filter. Then 20px. It is a status dot or an avatar. Then 50%, and it stays square in aspect. It is a diagram marker or a numbered legend bullet. Then 50%. Nothing else qualifies. A badge is not a chip, and it stays at 2px.

{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.b }}
An icon here is a line drawing in a single colour, and it exists to make a destination findable at a glance — never to decorate a label that already reads.
There are two families and they do not mix: the glyph, drawn on a 40 grid for navigation and section identity, and the inline icon, drawn on a 24 grid to sit beside a line of running text. Which one you want is a question of where the mark sits, not how large you want it — a glyph shrunk to 16px and an inline icon blown up to 22px are both wrong, because the stroke stops matching the type it stands next to.
01 Families TWO GRIDS
FAMILY WHEN
{{ f.n }} {{ f.el }} {{ f.spec }}
{{ f.b }}
There is no third family and no filled family. A solid shape in this system means a state — a status dot, the centre mark of a glyph — so an entirely filled icon would read as something switched on.
02 The set TWELVE · FIVE
GLYPHS · 40 GRID STROKE 2.2
{{ g.el }} {{ g.name }} {{ g.use }}
INLINE · 24 GRID STROKE 2
{{ i.el }} {{ i.name }} {{ i.use }}
Seventeen marks total, and the number is meant to stay small. A workspace that needs a thirteenth glyph usually needs a clearer name instead — a drawing cannot rescue a destination nobody can describe.
03 Construction FIVE RULES
{{ c }}
04 Usage DRAW · DON'T
Use an icon when
The thing is a place you return to, and you will scan for it rather than read for it. The rail can collapse, so the mark has to carry the row on its own. A row of siblings needs to be told apart at speed — dock, palette, menu. The label is a verb you use constantly and the mark is already a convention.
Use words instead when
The item is a page name — Subnav is deliberately iconless. The action is destructive or irreversible. Then the word leads and the mark follows. The concept is abstract enough that two designers would draw it differently. You are filling space. An icon added for rhythm is noise with a stroke width.

{{ icoDrainEl2 }}

✓ One colour throughout. Every line survives a light theme and a 1× screen equally.

09 Changelog THREE RELEASES
{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.b }}
A shadow in this system does not mean important. It means temporary — this thing has left the page and can be dismissed.
Every surface that belongs to the layout sits flat: cards, panels, tables, rails, the header. Separation between them is a hairline, never a shadow, because a raised card promises a dismiss that is not there. The four levels below are therefore not a scale of importance — they are four distances a floating thing can be from the page, and each one is spoken for by a single kind of overlay. Depth is not decoration here; it is the only visual cue that Escape will do something.
01 Levels FOUR · LOCKED
LEVEL WHEN
Flat none
Everything in the layout. Cards, panels, tables, the dock, the subnav, the header — all of it sits on the background with a hairline for separation. This is the default and it covers the overwhelming majority of surfaces, which is why the page reads as one plane rather than a stack of trays.
Bubble Duplicate 0 12px 30px rgba(0,0,0,.5)
Tooltip, and nothing else. The shortest throw in the set because the bubble has to stay visually attached to the control it names — lift it any further and it starts to read as a menu you could click.
Menu 0 22px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.45)
Anything anchored to a trigger: Select, Multi-select, Popover, the account menu, a table row's overflow. It floats free of the page but stays tied to a position on it, so it takes no scrim — the page behind is still legible and still the context. Toast takes this throw too, despite sitting at the top of the z ladder: it is pinned to a corner rather than to a trigger, but it is the same kind of small, self-dismissing thing, and giving it the overlay throw would make a passing confirmation look like a question.
Overlay 0 30px 90px rgba(0,0,0,.5)
Modal, Drawer and the command bar — the three things that take the whole screen hostage. The drawer runs the same throw on its horizontal axis, -30px 0 90px, so a panel entering from the right casts its shadow back across the page it covers rather than downward onto nothing.
There is no level between Menu and Overlay, and no level for a card. If a surface seems to need one, it is usually a surface that wants to be an overlay and has not committed — or a hairline that was never drawn.
02 Scrim BLUR, NOT BLACK
SURFACE RECIPE WHY
{{ s.n }} {{ s.v }} {{ s.b }}
A scrim is a tinted blur of the page's own background, never a black wash. Black would flatten the amber and read as a different product; blurring the page keeps the operator's place visible while making it plainly out of reach.
03 The z ladder FIVE STOPS
{{ z.z }} {{ z.n }} {{ z.b }}
Five stops, wide apart on purpose: the gaps leave room for a local raise inside a component without anything needing to renegotiate with the ladder. A new value is a design decision, not a bug fix — there is no z-index 81.
04 Pressure NOT ELEVATION
HOVER HOVER
translateY(-1px) · 0 3px 10px -4px rgba(0,0,0,.45) · primary: 0 4px 12px -4px color-mix(in oklab,var(--accent),transparent 45%) A one-pixel lift with a tight shadow. It is feedback on a control, not a change of layer — which is why the throw is a tenth of the Menu level and disappears the moment the pointer leaves. The primary button casts the same lift in amber rather than black, because a neutral shadow under a saturated fill reads as dirt.
PRESS PRESS
translateY(1px) scale(.985) · inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,.35) · primary: inset 0 2px 5px color-mix(in oklab,black,transparent 60%) The two inset shadows in the system, and both of them are presses. Press is the mirror of hover — down instead of up — so a control that lifts on hover must sink on press, or the click has no landing. The primary's inset is a hair deeper because it has to darken an already-bright fill.
Neither value belongs to the level set, and neither may be reused on a surface that is not a control. The focus ring is also a box-shadow — a 2px background gap plus a 4px amber halo — but it is a ring, not a shadow: it does not move the element and it is owned by Accessibility.
05 Usage RAISE · DON'T
Raise it when
The thing appeared in response to an action and will go away again. It covers content it did not push aside, so its edges must be readable against anything. Escape or a click outside will dismiss it. Elevation is the promise; the handler is the delivery. It escapes its parent's bounds — a menu on the last table row cannot be clipped.
Keep it flat when
It is part of the page and stays there — every Card and panel. You want to signal importance. That is Color's job, or a heavier border. You are separating two adjacent surfaces. A 1px hairline is the tool, and it goes first. The surface scrolls with the content. A shadow that scrolls reads as a rendering error.

RUNS
214 finished
✕ Cards floated on overlay shadows. Nothing here is dismissible, so the depth is a lie.
Discard run?
✓ Overlay level plus a blurred scrim. The page stays visible but is clearly out of reach.
Discard run?
✕ A black wash with no shadow. The context is gone and the panel has no edge to speak of.
STATUS
Running Paused
✓ Menu level, anchored to its trigger, no scrim. The page behind is still the context.
STATUS
Running Paused
✕ Overlay throw on a select. It reads as a modal, so the operator waits for a scrim that never comes.

10 Changelog THREE RELEASES
{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.b }}
Motion here has one job: to say what just changed, and where it came from. Nothing moves to be admired.
This is a console an operator watches for hours, so the budget is spent on transitions that carry cause and effect — a panel arriving from the direction it was summoned, a row acknowledging a click. Everything else holds still. Two things may loop and only two: something that is genuinely live, and something that is genuinely waiting. A third looping element in a view means one of them is decoration, and decoration in peripheral vision reads as an alert.
01 Durations FIVE STEPS · THREE STRAYS
STEP WHEN
{{ d.n }} · {{ d.v }} {{ d.e }}
{{ d.b }}
Bars are drawn to scale against the 900ms Draw ceiling. These five are the scale; 140 and 180 are the only neighbours close enough to argue about, and they never appear on the same element. Three further values are still in the codebase and are not part of it: 160ms on the dock's active rail, the radio dot, the swatch border and the select caret; 200ms on the dock labels; and 220ms on every launcher tile. Each is a chrome timing that predates the scale and should collapse into Instant, Control or Panel — they are listed here because a spec that quietly omits what ships is not a spec.
02 Easing THREE CURVES
ease 140ms · 180ms — hover, chips, rows, controls The browser default, kept deliberately for the short steps. At 140ms no curve is legible anyway, and reaching for a custom bezier on something this brief is a decision nobody can see.
cubic-bezier(.4, 0, .2, 1) 260ms · 500ms — panels, layout, entrances Everything long enough to watch. It leaves quickly and arrives slowly, which is what makes a panel feel like it was placed rather than thrown. The Draw step uses .35, 0, .2, 1 — the same shape with a fractionally softer start, because a line being drawn should not appear to snap off its origin.
cubic-bezier(.45, 0, .55, 1) 1.8s — the waiting sweep, looping The only symmetrical curve, and it exists for one reason: a loop has no end. An asymmetric ease arriving slowly and then restarting at speed produces a visible jerk at the seam, so anything that repeats forever accelerates and decelerates by equal amounts.
No easing in this system overshoots. There is no spring, no bounce and no elastic curve — an overshoot implies weight and play, and nothing in an operations console should feel like it has momentum of its own.
03 Entrances SIX · ONCE EACH
NAME FROM WHERE
{{ e.n }} {{ e.v }} {{ e.b }}
Every entrance travels a short distance on one axis and fades — 6px for a small element, 12–16px for a panel. Nothing scales up from zero, and nothing rotates in. No card or panel entrance is delayed: a group of equals shares one duration and arrives together, and where a group mixes panel weights the heavier one is given 50ms more to settle. Delay is reserved for visualization geometry and its labels. Geometry steps 40 to 130ms per element — 40ms across the fine grid lines of a node graph, 130ms between the rings of a research map, wider the heavier the thing being drawn — while labels step 55 to 90ms over a 520–900ms base, so a name never arrives before the shape it belongs to. A six-layer signals chart runs 110ms per layer, putting the last line 550ms behind the first. That is deliberate: a chart is meant to be watched once, and a grid of cards is not.
04 Loops LIVE OR WAITING
3 AGENTS LIVE
pulse · 2.6s ease-in-out infinite Live status. The period is slow on purpose — a 2.6-second breath reads as a heartbeat in peripheral vision, where anything under a second reads as an alarm. One pulse per view.
sweepline · 1.8s cubic-bezier(.45,0,.55,1) infinite · .22s stagger Indeterminate waiting, and it stops the instant a real number is available. A sweep that outlives its own request is the most expensive animation in the system, because it teaches the operator to ignore movement.
The full loop set is pulse at 2.6s and breathe at 2s for live status — 1.1s where breathe carries a working label rather than a state — then sweepline, shimmer, ringspin and caretblink for waiting, and gridDrift and glowdrift for the ambient background of the launcher — the one place decoration is allowed, because there is nothing there to read yet. Where several tracks sweep together they are staggered .22s apart so the group reads as one movement.
05 Usage MOVE · HOLD
Animate when
Something arrives or leaves, and the direction says where it came from. A control needs to acknowledge a pointer or a key within 180ms. The layout itself changes size — the dock collapsing, a drawer taking width. The system is genuinely working and cannot yet say how far along it is.
Hold still when
The content is the point. Numbers never count up; a table never reflows for effect. You want to draw attention — that is Color, and it works without moving. Something already animates nearby. Two loops in one view is one too many. The element is under a pointer that is about to click it. Nothing should move away.
06 Do and don't THREE PAIRS · LIVE
Ingest · running
Normalize · queued
Export · paused
✓ One pulse for the one live thing. Movement means running, so the eye goes straight to it.
Ingest · running
Normalize · queued
Export · paused
✕ Three loops at three periods. Nothing is emphasised, and a paused row appears to be working.
Hover me · 140ms
✓ Instant on hover. The row answers before you have finished arriving on it.
Hover me · 800ms
✕ A reveal-length curve on a hover. The control feels broken, then feels slow.
✓ Skeletons hold still; one sweep carries the waiting. The geometry is already correct.
✕ Every bar shimmering at once. Three loops where one would do, and the eye cannot settle.

10 Changelog THREE RELEASES
{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.b }}
A chart in this system is a drawn object with a name, not a configuration of a charting library.
Eight forms exist, each one answering a different question about shape of data, and asking for one by name is how a chart gets specified. This page owns what they share — the projection they are drawn on, the colour rule, how a reader is meant to decode them, and the accessibility floor they currently fall short of. What any single form encodes, and where it breaks, belongs to that form's own page. The boundary against Progress is worth stating once: a chart plots a set of values in a coordinate space, and Progress plots one fraction against a known total.
01 The forms EIGHT · SEVEN ISOMETRIC
NAME ENCODES IN USE
{{ f.n }} {{ f.e }} {{ f.w }}
The names are the interface. Each one states an encoding rather than a look, so choosing between them is a question about the data and not about taste — a Ridge and a Column series both plot time, and the difference is whether you are comparing windows or reading one line. The set is open: a ninth form joins it by earning a name on the same terms.
02 The engine ONE PROJECTION
Block field HOVER A BLOCK
{{ dsVizEl }}
There is no WebGL and no 3D library. Every solid is plain SVG on a faked isometric projection, and one function maps (x, y, z) to the plane:
X = ox + (x − z) · cos30 · s
Y = oy + (x + z) · sin30 · s − y · s
A solid is three polygons — top, left and right face — at descending fill opacity, which is what reads as light without a light source. Lines draw themselves once through pathLength=1 and an animated stroke-dashoffset. The viewBox is computed from the projected bounds of the geometry, so an object always centres in its panel no matter how the data changes shape.
Depth s and the projection origin are the only per-form parameters. A new isometric form is written against this function rather than beside it — a second projection would mean two visual languages sharing one page.
03 Series colour TWO IS THE CEILING
This period Prior period
{{ b.label }}
Amber carries the value being judged and Ice carries whatever it is judged against — prior period, baseline, forecast. Two is the ceiling, and it is a ceiling rather than a default: the seven isometric forms are all single-series, and only Comparison bars spends the second colour. A third series is not a colour problem, it is a sign the chart has been asked more than one question. Series also separate by lightness and position, never by hue alone.
04 Reading rules FIVE
{{ r.n }} {{ r.b }}
One chart per screen, in the primary panel, for a quantity worth contemplating — load, coverage, throughput, backlog. Where a number or a bar answers the question, the number wins, and a chart never appears as decoration on a form or a list.

This page is not a checklist to be audited against later. It is the set of floors every other foundation was built on top of.
The reasoning runs one way: the grey ramp exists because four levels of text had to clear their ratios in both themes, amber owns action because it is the one hue that holds under deuteranopia, and the loop set is two long because a third moving thing in peripheral vision is indistinguishable from an alarm. So the rules below are not additions to the system — removing any one of them would require redrawing Color, Motion or Icons. Every figure here is enforced somewhere else and cross-referenced to it.
01 Contrast MEASURED LIVE
TOKEN ON --BG DARK / LIGHT
TOKEN USE DARK LIGHT GRADE
{{ c.n }} {{ c.use }} {{ c.d }} {{ c.l }} {{ c.grade }}
Ratios are computed from the live token values against --bg in each theme and graded on the worse of the two, so a token cannot pass here by being good in dark and marginal in light. The ramp was tuned until this table came out clean rather than the other way round — which is why --faint is the one level restricted by use, not by ratio: it clears the large-text threshold and nothing more, so it carries captions and never sentences.
02 Focus TWO TREATMENTS
RUN SWEEP
0 0 0 2px var(--bg), 0 0 0 4px var(--accent-line) Buttons, rows, tiles, links — everything that is not a field. Two rings: a 2px gap in the page background, then 2px of amber. The gap is what makes the halo survive on a filled button and against a hairline, where a single ring would be swallowed by the border it sits on.
sweep—nightly|
border --accent-line · 0 0 0 3px var(--accent-soft) Inputs, textareas, selects and any control that takes a caret. A soft amber wash instead of a hard ring, because a field already has a border to recolour and a hard halo around a text box reads as an error state.

03 Hit targets 32 DENSE · 44 PRIMARY
MARK TARGET HOW
{{ t.n }} {{ t.v }} {{ t.b }}
The visual mark shrinks; the target does not. Every figure in the middle column is the measured box around the mark, never the mark itself — which is why a 7px status dot and a 54px table row are the same click. These are the numbers the running product computes, not the ones the stylesheet intends: the two diverge the moment a flex parent is allowed to shrink its children, which is a defect rather than a decision.
04 Colour is never alone THREE CARRIERS
Running
A word beside the dot. Status is never the colour of a circle alone — amber and grey are a hue apart, but "running" and "queued" are unambiguous.
Selected
A mark inside the fill. Selection carries a checkmark, so the state survives a monochrome screen and a printed page alike.
Current T−10s T−20s
A legend on the series. Chart layers separate by lightness as well as hue, and every one is named — no reading depends on telling two greys apart.
Amber and ice differ in hue and in lightness, so they hold apart under deuteranopia and protanopia rather than relying on either axis alone. That is the reason the palette has two accents and not four — a third would have to sit between them on both axes at once.
05 Reduced motion PER LOOP
MOTION BECOMES WHAT CARRIES IT INSTEAD
{{ m.n }} {{ m.v }} {{ m.b }}
The test is simple: switch every animation off and nothing should become unreadable or unknowable. That constraint is why no state in this system is expressed by movement in the first place — reduced motion removes emphasis, never information.

Text is two typefaces and four weights of grey, and every other typographic decision is already made.
Space Grotesk sets headings and numerals; IBM Plex Mono sets everything else, which is why this shell reads like an instrument rather than a document. There is no separate colour for emphasis: importance is carried by the grey ramp — --fg, --dim, --mute, --faint — and amber is reserved for things that act. Bold and italic are not part of the system.

02 Roles SIX
ROLE WHEN
Display Calm Grotesk 600 · 34–48px
One per screen, at the top of a page or a home hero. It is the only place the type is allowed to be large, and it is always a statement rather than a label.
Heading Everything nominal Grotesk 600 · 17–28px
Names a panel, a card or a section. Sentence case, no terminal punctuation, and never more than one line — if it wraps, it is doing the body’s job.
Body Four stages finished inside their windows. Mono 14px / 1.6 · --dim
The explaining voice. Two or three lines at a measure of about 70 characters; past that the paragraph is a document and belongs somewhere the operator has chosen to read.
Label Panel label Mono 12px · .16em caps
Names a region or a column. The tracking is what makes caps readable at this size, and it is the reason labels are two or three words at most.
Caption SYS·00 · 2m ago Mono 10.5–11px · .2em
Machine facts: codes, counts, timestamps, the // phase voice. It is the smallest type in the system and the only role allowed to be --faint, because nothing depends on reading it.
Numeral 214 Grotesk 600 · tabular
Any number the operator reads as a value rather than as prose. Grotesk for the figures, tabular so a column of them lines up, and never coloured to imply good or bad on its own.
There is no bold body, no italic, and no third typeface. Emphasis inside a paragraph is a step up the grey ramp to --fg and nothing else — a system with one weight of emphasis never has to decide which of two emphases wins.
Live — the ramp and the states ROLES & STATES
HEADING
Everything nominal
BODY
Body copy is mono at 12.5px with 1.6 line-height. Keep paragraphs under three lines — this shell is for scanning, not reading.

Panel label Micro caption · SYS·00
EMPHASIS
Primary — --fg Secondary — --dim Muted — --mute Faint — captions only
STATES
Link — accent, no underline Error — inline validation Completed — struck through Disabled — 50% opacity inline code
03 Usage THE GREY RAMP
Reach for the ramp when
One thing in a block matters more than the rest — move it up, not bigger. A line is supporting detail — --mute says so without shrinking it. The text is a machine fact nobody has to read — that is --faint. Two lines sit side by side and one is the answer — the ramp ranks them.
Reach for something else when
The text is a system-assigned status — that is a Badge. The text acts when pressed — that is a Button or a link. There is no content to describe — that is an Empty state. The paragraph runs past four lines — it needs a document, not a panel.

A card is a bounded surface that holds one thing worth looking at on its own.
It draws an edge around content so a page can be read as a set of objects rather than one column of text. A card stays flat in the page and stays put — the moment content needs to float over everything else it is a Modal, and when rows share the same fields and want comparing it is a Table. Only one kind of card is clickable, and that is the exception, not the default.

03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The content is one whole object that makes sense read on its own. A page holds several such objects and the reader needs to tell where one ends. The grouping is stable — the same card appears in the same place tomorrow. It sits in the page flow, at the page's own scroll position.
Use something else when
It must float over the page and be dismissed — that is a Modal. Every item shares the same fields and wants comparing — that is a Table. The box would hold a single label — that is a Badge or a heading. There is nothing to show yet — that is an Empty state, not a bordered void.

04 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The click commits something — data is written, a job starts, a record is destroyed. The operator chose to act, rather than being told about something. The action can be named as a verb the operator would use out loud. It belongs to the view it sits in, not to a row inside it.
Use something else when
It only changes which panel is visible — that is Navigation (Tabs). It carries a value the operator picked or can dismiss — that is a Chip. It flips one setting on or off in place — that is a Switch. It navigates somewhere else — that is a link, styled as text.

A text input is one line the operator types into, and the box every other field in the system is measured against.
Select, multi-select and textarea all inherit its border, radius, padding and height, so a form of mixed controls reads as one column of boxes rather than a collection of parts. It holds a value the operator authors, which is the line against every picker: if the legal answers are known in advance, hiding them behind free text is a trap. Anything longer than a line is a Textarea.

03 Usage AUTHORED VALUES
Use when
The operator authors the value and only they know it — a name, a key, a query. The answer is short enough to read back in one line. The legal answers cannot be listed in advance. Typing is genuinely faster than choosing, as it is in search.
Use something else when
The answers are a known list — that is a Select or a Radio group. The value runs past one line — that is a Textarea. The answer is yes or no — that is a Checkbox or a Switch. The typing filters what is on screen right now — that is the command bar, not a form field.

A checkbox records an independent yes-or-no the operator sets themselves.
Each box stands on its own, so ticking one says nothing about the others, and nothing happens until the form is submitted. If the options are mutually exclusive it is a Radio; if the change lands the instant it is flipped it is a Switch. That deferred, independent quality is what everything below assumes.

03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The answer is independently yes or no, and other options do not constrain it. The operator may pick none, some, or all of a small set. The change is committed later by a submit, not the instant it is clicked. The full set of options is short enough to show at once — up to about seven.
Use something else when
Exactly one option may be chosen — that is a Radio. The setting applies immediately with no submit — that is a Switch. The list is long or the chosen set must stay visible — that is Select (Multi). It selects rows to act on rather than recording a value — that belongs to Table, where selection is Ice.

A radio group is a set of mutually exclusive options, all visible at once, exactly one of them chosen.
It exists so the operator can compare the alternatives before committing, which is why it costs vertical space and why it stops being the right control past about five options. The line against Checkbox is arithmetic: checkboxes are independent and can all be off, radios are one-of and can never be none. If “none” is a legitimate answer, it has to be an option in the list rather than an empty group.

03 Usage TWO TO FIVE OPTIONS
Use when
Two to five options, exactly one of which will be true. The options need comparing before choosing — seeing them all is the point. The choice is part of a form and commits with everything else. The wording of each option matters more than the space it costs.
Use something else when
Six or more options, or a list that grows — that is Select. Several can be true at once — that is Checkbox. It is one setting on or off, committing instantly — that is a Switch. The choice filters a list rather than setting a value — those are Chips.

A switch turns one thing on or off, and the change takes effect the moment it moves.
That instant commit is the entire difference from a Checkbox, which records an answer and waits for a submit. A switch has no submit to wait for, so it belongs in settings and toolbars rather than in forms, and it must never appear beside a Save button that implies it was holding its breath. It is also always one thing: two switches offered as alternatives are a Radio group in the wrong clothes.

A multi-select holds several values in one field, each one a token the operator can take back out.

It is still a form control, not a filter bar — if the choice narrows a list in front of the operator, those are Chips.

03 Usage WHEN THE TOTAL IS KNOWN
Use when
The system can count both what is done and what is left. The work runs long enough that the operator would otherwise wonder — roughly five seconds and up. The fraction is a level worth knowing on its own: quota, coverage, capacity. The stages are named and discrete, and finishing one is the news.
Use something else when
The total is unknown — that is Loading, with a phase label. The work is instant; a bar that flashes is noise, not feedback. The result is already in and only needs reporting — that is a Toast. The number is the point and the shape adds nothing — write the count as text.

A Block field plots one count across a handful of named areas, as solids standing on a shared floor.
It answers “where is the weight” and nothing else. The nearest neighbour is Column series, and the difference is what the horizontal axis means: a Column series spaces its solids by time and can be read as a trend, while a Block field spaces them by category, where left-to-right carries no order beyond the one the caller chose. Reading a slope across a Block field is always a mistake.

A Node map draws a topology — workflows as diamond markers on stems, connected by lines that state only that one hands off to another.
It is the system’s only form for structure that branches. Every other chart lays its subjects along one axis; a Node map is for when the real shape of the data is a graph, and the useful thing to show is which parts connect to which — with one node, at most, flagged as the one that needs attention.

04 Usage ONE FLAG AT A TIME
Use when
The subjects genuinely branch — a pipeline, a dependency graph, an org of agents. Which parts connect to which is itself the thing worth showing. At most one node needs to be called out as the one to look at. Four to eight nodes, so the connections stay a shape rather than a tangle.
Use something else when
The parts are a fixed, linear sequence — that is a Plate stack. The structure is concentric, not branching — that is Ring coverage. More than one node needs flagging — draw one map per flag, or use a Table. Every node’s exact status matters at once — a Table scales past eight rows where this map cannot.

{{ ndBadFlag }}

{{ l.v }} {{ l.d }} {{ l.c }}
Ring coverage nests concentric ellipses, each one a thread of sources, narrowing to a single amber ring at the centre.
It exists for containment, not connection — every ring wholly encloses the one inside it, which is what separates it from Node map’s arbitrary branching. Radius stands for the size of a thread’s source pool; depth toward the centre stands for how worked that thread is. The two are independent, and only one ring — the innermost — ever carries the accent.

04 Usage ONE CORE AT A TIME
Use when
Coverage genuinely narrows from broad to specific — a research thread, a filter funnel, a triage pass. Every thread wholly contains the ones inside it. Overlapping-but-not-nested sets need a different form. One thread is the deepest or most-worked, and worth naming as the core. Three to five threads, so the inner rings stay distinguishable shells.
Use something else when
The relationships branch rather than nest — that is a Node map. The set is a fixed, unrelated sequence — that is a Plate stack. Every thread’s exact source count matters at once — a Table scales past five rows where this cannot. The pools genuinely overlap rather than nest — this form will misrepresent them as containment.

A City grid plots one quantity across two spatial axes — region as column, instance as row — as a skyline of solids on a shared scale.
It is Block field with a second axis: where a field has only categories to group by, a City grid has categories and instances within them, and every node in the whole grid is measured against the same range. It is also the only form in this set that allows more than one flagged cell at once.

04 Usage ANY NUMBER OF FLAGS
Use when
The data genuinely has two axes — a region and an instance within it, a rack and a slot, a grid and a cell. Every node shares one scale, so comparing across regions is meaningful. Zero, one or several cells may need flagging at once. Three to six regions, each a handful of instances deep.
Use something else when
There is only one axis to group by — that is a Block field. The nodes relate to each other rather than sitting in independent regional columns — that is a Node map. Every node’s exact load matters at once — a Table scales past six regions where this grid cannot. The measure is a single time series, not a spatial grid — that is a Column series.

A tooltip names the thing under the pointer, in one line, and holds nothing the operator has to reach.
It exists so an icon can stay an icon. Because it appears on hover and takes no pointer events, everything inside it is unreachable by definition — no links, no buttons, no selectable text. That is the whole line against Popover: the moment content has to be clicked, the trigger has to be clicked too. And a tooltip never carries information that exists nowhere else, because a pointer is one of several ways to use this shell.

03 Usage NAMES, NOT NEWS
Use when
An icon-only control needs its name spelled out. A truncated cell needs its full value on demand. A keyboard shortcut is worth showing next to the control it fires. The information is a convenience — the operator can work without ever seeing it.
Use something else when
Anything inside has to be clicked — that is a Popover. The text explains a field’s constraint — that is the field’s own hint line. It says why a control is locked — that belongs beside the control, in the layout. It reports something that just happened — that is a Toast.

A popover is a small surface anchored to the control that opened it, holding actions or detail that would otherwise clutter the page.
It is opened by a click, dismissed by looking away, and it never blocks the page behind it. That is the line against Modal: a modal is centred, scrimmed and must be answered before work continues, while a popover is peripheral and costs nothing to abandon. Against Tooltip the line is the click — anything that opens on hover is a tooltip and may contain nothing the operator has to reach.

The header is the 52px bar pinned to the top of every screen, naming the selected module and carrying ambient reference and the operator’s own identity.
It is chrome, not content: it says where you are in the product and who you are signed in as, and nothing about the page underneath. That is the line against the page header inside the content column — breadcrumb, title, status, actions all live there, because they change with the route. Anything that would need to change when the operator navigates does not belong in this bar.

02 Zones THREE
ZONE WHAT IT MAY HOLD
Module title COMPONENTS SYS·02 --accent · rail glyph
The selected top-level rail item — its own glyph, name and a SYS code — anchoring the left edge that the brand lockup vacated. It only ever names the top level; it never follows the operator into a sub-page.
Ambient {{ date }} {{ clock }} --dim / --mute
Date then clock, split by a 1px 12px divider. Reference only — nothing in this zone is clickable, and nothing in it is ever amber, because a workspace where the wall clock competes with an alert is a workspace nobody reads.
Identity 34px · --accent dot
A 34px square opening the operator menu — appearance, preferences, sign out. The status dot is the single live element in the whole bar, which is what makes it readable at a glance.
There is no search field, no notification tray and no page action in this bar, and no compact variant of it. Global search belongs to the command palette on a keystroke; alerts belong to the surface that owns them; a page’s primary action belongs beside that page’s title. Nothing here changes with the route below it — not even the module title, which tracks the rail, not the page.
LIVE — 52PX, TRANSLUCENT, OVER SCROLLING CONTENT
{{ date }} {{ clock }}
A blurred 60% background over the page, so content stays visible as it passes underneath. The 1px bottom hairline is the only hard edge the bar owns.

Belongs in the bar
Ambient reference the operator glances at rather than acts on. Who is signed in, and the menu that changes that. State that is true on every screen, at every route, without exception.
Belongs somewhere else
Where the operator is, and what the page is called — that is the page header. Moving between workspaces — that is Navigation (Main). Moving within one — that is Navigation (Subnav). Anything that has just happened — that is a Toast.

The main rail is the full-height column on the left that moves the operator between workspaces.
It is the only navigation in the product that never changes: the same items, in the same order, on every screen. That fixity is the point — it is hit fifty times a day and must be answerable by muscle memory rather than by reading. The line against Navigation (Subnav) is scope: the rail chooses which workspace you are in, the subnav chooses where you are inside it. One level each, and neither borrows the other’s job.

02 Widths and states TWO WIDTHS · FOUR STATES
WIDTH WHEN
Expanded 216px · icon + label
The default, and what a new operator sees. Labels are what make the rail learnable, so it starts open and stays open unless the operator chooses otherwise.
Collapsed 56px · icon only
For operators who know the rail by shape and want the width back for their work. Every item stays present and in the same order — only the labels leave, into a native tooltip. The content shifts by exactly the difference over 260ms.
There is no flyout, no nested tree and no “more” overflow. A rail that hides items behind a second interaction is no longer answerable by memory, and a second level of nesting is what the subnav is for.

The subnav is the column of pages inside one workspace, docked to the right of the main rail.
It is the only navigation in the product that changes with the route: a different workspace means a different list, and the list is the workspace’s own table of contents. The line against Navigation (Tabs) is what happens when you click. A subnav row loads a different page, with its own URL and its own header; a tab swaps the view of the page you are already on. If leaving the row would lose unsaved work in the panel beside it, it was a tab.

03 Usage RECORDS, NOT NUMBERS
Use when
Rows are records with a stable identity the operator acts on. The same action is often wanted on several rows at once. Four to seven facts per row decide what to do next. Scanning down one column is a real task — status, owner, last run.
Use something else when
Each item needs an image, a summary, or free-form text — those are Cards. There is nothing to act on and nothing to compare — that is a list. The point is the shape of the numbers — that is a Visualization. There are no rows yet — that is an Empty state, in place of the body.

A toast reports what just happened, in the corner, and leaves on its own.
It is the cheapest surface in the system: it takes no focus, blocks nothing, and asks for nothing. That is also its limit — anything the operator must read or answer cannot be a toast, because it will be gone in 3.2 seconds and it was never in their way. A decision belongs in a Modal; a standing condition belongs in the panel that owns it, not in a corner that empties itself.

03 Usage REPORT, NEVER ASK
Use when
Something finished and the operator would otherwise not know. The outcome is worth a sentence but not worth their attention. The result arrived out of band — a background run, a sync, a queue. Missing the message costs nothing, because the state is legible elsewhere.
Use something else when
The operator has to decide something — that is a Modal. The message must survive being missed — that belongs in the panel that owns the state. It annotates a row or a field — that is a Badge or an inline error. Work is still running — that is Progress, which stays until it finishes.

A Callout reports a standing condition inside the panel or flow it belongs to, and stays until the operator acts on it or clears it.
It is Toast’s persistent counterpart: where a toast reports what just happened and leaves on its own in 3.2 seconds, a Callout stays exactly because the condition it names is still true. That is also the line against Modal — a Callout never blocks the rest of the page, and if the operator must answer before doing anything else, the message needed a modal, not a card.

03 Usage STANDING, NOT MOMENTARY
Use when
A condition is standing, not momentary — it should still be true if the operator looks back in five minutes. The message belongs inside the panel or flow it is about, not floating over everything. Zero, one or two actions are enough to resolve or acknowledge it.
Use something else when
The news is transient and does not need to persist — that is a Toast. The operator must answer before doing anything else — that is a Modal. The fact is a small, permanent label on a row — that is a Badge, not a card.

{{ coGoodTitle }}
✓ Title states the fact plainly. An operator scanning the panel knows exactly what happened without reading the body.
{{ coBadTitle }}
✕ A feelings-first title and casual body read as unfinished copy, not a system report — name the fact, not the reaction to it.
{{ coGoodActions }}
✓ One action, unstyled as secondary since nothing here is urgent enough to demand a primary button.
{{ coBadActions }}
✕ Two actions with no clear primary compete for attention — a warning this routine should offer at most one way forward.
{{ coGoodTone }}
✓ Error tone on a run that stopped and needs a decision. Colour, icon and copy all agree.
{{ coBadTone }}
✕ The same failure in the Success tone — amber and a checkmark on a message that says nothing finished. Tone must match the state, not the writer\u2019s mood.
06 Accessibility FOUR
Role by tone Warning and Error carry role="alert" so assistive tech announces them on arrival. Info and Success carry role="status", announced politely without interrupting.
Colour never alone Every tone pairs its colour with a distinct icon shape and states its own severity in words — "Retry" and "no action required yet" carry the finding on their own.
Focus order Actions are reachable by keyboard in the order shown, primary first. A dismiss control, when present, is always last in the tab order.
Never auto-dismissed Unlike Toast, a Callout never times out on its own — if it should disappear by itself, it was a Toast to begin with.
07 Tokens FIVE
--accent-2Info icon and title.
--accent, --accent-softSuccess icon, title and fill — the one tone sharing the acting colour.
#ff8f6b (soft)Warning icon and border at reduced opacity, no fill.
#ff8f6b (full)Error icon, border and a low-opacity fill — the same hue as Warning, one step stronger.
--dimBody text across every tone.
08 Related FOUR
Toast The transient counterpart. Reach for Toast when the message should be gone in a few seconds on its own.
Modal Where a Callout escalates once a decision must block everything else on the page.
Badge The flat alternative. A one-word status on a row is a badge before it is ever a card.
Cards The container a Callout usually sits inside, rather than replaces.

v1.0.018 Sep 2026 First specification. Named Callout to sit next to Toast without colliding, and given a Warning tone Toast deliberately omits — built from the same accent and #ff8f6b tokens Toast already established, split into two intensities rather than a new hue, to keep the amber-and-one-other-colour rule intact.
A modal is a centred dialog that stops the workspace until the operator answers it.
It is the most expensive surface in the system, because it takes away every other choice on the screen. That cost is the whole reason it exists: a decision that must not be missed. The line against a Drawer is whether the work behind may continue — a drawer accompanies, a modal interrupts. If the operator could reasonably ignore it for a minute and carry on, it was never a modal.

03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The action is destructive or irreversible and deserves a deliberate pause. Nothing else on the screen makes sense until this is answered. The whole decision fits on one screen with no internal scrolling. There are exactly two ways out, and both are named.
Use something else when
The work behind stays relevant — that is a Drawer. It is a few choices anchored to the control that opened it — that is a Popover. It only reports that something happened — that is a Toast. It is a form with sections, or anything that scrolls — that is a drawer or a page.

A drawer is a full-height panel that slides in from the right and sits beside the work instead of on top of it.
It is the surface for detail, settings and editing — anything where the page behind stays relevant and the operator should still be able to read it. That is the line against a Modal: a modal interrupts and demands one answer before anything else happens, while a drawer accompanies. If the operator can safely keep looking at the table they came from, it is a drawer.

03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The operator is inspecting or editing one record while the list it came from stays useful. The content is longer than a modal should be — a form with sections, an activity log, a config. They will move through several records in turn, and reopening a centred dialog each time would be punishing. The work behind must remain readable for reference while the panel is open.
Use something else when
One decision must be made before anything else can proceed — that is a Modal. It is a short set of choices anchored to the control that opened it — that is a Popover. The content deserves its own address and history entry — that is a page. It is only confirming that something happened — that is a Toast.

An empty state is what a region says when it has loaded successfully and has nothing to show.
It is a statement of fact with a way forward, not an apology and not decoration. The line against Loading is certainty: loading means the answer is unknown, empty means the answer is known and it is none. Showing an empty state while a request is still in flight is the one failure mode that matters here, because it tells the operator to act on a conclusion the system has not reached.

02 Variants THREE KINDS
KIND WHEN
First run No workflows yet NEW WORKFLOW primary action
Nothing exists yet because nothing has been made. This is the only kind that earns a primary button, because creating the first record is genuinely the next thing to do.
No results No runs match FAILED CLEAR FILTER ghost action
Records exist, but the operator’s own query excluded them. Name the filter that did it and offer to undo it — the way out is backwards, not forwards, so the action is a ghost.
Restricted Not visible to you Ask the workspace owner for access. no action
There is content, but not for this operator. Say so plainly and name who can change it. Offering a button they cannot use is worse than offering none.
There is no error variant and no illustrated variant. A failed request is not empty — it gets an inline error with a retry, because “nothing here” would quietly turn a broken system into a normal one. And art in place of data reads as celebration; a 22px hairline glyph is as much decoration as this system allows.

03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The request finished and the result is legitimately nothing. A region would otherwise be a blank rectangle with no explanation. There is a clear next step, or a clear reason there is none. The operator’s own filter is why they see nothing, and they may not remember setting it.
Use something else when
The answer is not known yet — that is Loading. The request failed — that is an inline error with a retry. Something was completed and needs acknowledging — that is a Toast. Only one field of a filled record is blank — that is an em dash in the cell, not a state.

Loading is what a region shows while it still does not know the answer.
It is the only place in the system where amber moves without something having happened, and it earns that because motion is the one honest way to say “still working”. The line against Progress is knowledge: progress states a measured fraction of a known total, loading states nothing but that work is under way. Never fake one as the other — a bar creeping to 90% and stopping is worse than a sweep that admits it cannot say.
01 Anatomy FIVE PARTS

02 Variants THREE · BY WHAT IS KNOWN
VARIANT WHEN
Sweep stack --accent-line / --accent
The default, and the house style. Two or three hairlines of unequal width, staggered by 220ms, standing in for text that has not arrived. Use it when an agent is working and the shape of the answer is not yet known.
Skeleton --border / --border-2
For layouts whose shape is already known — table rows, a card grid. It holds the exact geometry the content will occupy so nothing jumps when it lands, and it is grey, not amber: the shape is the message, not the motion.
Inline caret // SYNCING 5×11px · 1s steps
For dense chrome where a stack will not fit: a table row mid-refresh, a button mid-submit, a status line. The phase name carries the meaning and the caret carries the liveness.
There is no spinner in this system, and no full-screen loading overlay. A rotating disc says only that something is happening somewhere, which the operator already assumed; and blanking the whole workspace to say it takes away the very context they were reading. Loading is always scoped to the region that is actually waiting.
LIVE — SCOPED TO ONE PANEL
Insight {{ loadPhaseMeta }}
{{ loadPhaseLabel }}
{{ p.label }}
The phase name is the part that does the work: it turns an indefinite wait into a report of what the system is actually doing.
03 Usage WHEN · WHEN NOT
Use when
The wait will exceed about 400ms — below that, showing anything only flickers. The duration cannot be measured, so no honest percentage exists. A named phase can be reported, and it will change as the work moves on. The region that is waiting can be pointed at precisely.
Use something else when
The total is known and the fraction is real — that is Progress. The work finished with nothing to show — that is an Empty state. The work finished and failed — that is an inline error with a retry. The work finished elsewhere and needs acknowledging — that is a Toast.

Badges
A badge is a static label that reports the state of the thing it sits beside.
It is assigned by the system, never by the operator, and it is never clickable.
Breadcrumb (11px, .2em, uppercase) sits above a 34px Space Grotesk title, then a status row, then the two-tier description: 19px --fg for what the thing is, 14px --mute for the line an operator could actually get wrong — usually the boundary against its nearest neighbour.
